name.text: Slice coverage definition

questiontext.text: In the Slice Coverage Explorer, slice coverage of a test suite is best defined as:

answer.text: The fraction of statements in the backward slice of the criterion variable that were executed

feedback.text: Correct — slice coverage counts how many statements of that backward slice a test suite exercises.

answer.text: The fraction of all executable statements executed by the suite

feedback.text: That is plain statement coverage; slice coverage is measured only over the slice.

answer.text: The fraction of branch outcomes taken, ignoring data flow

feedback.text: That is branch coverage; slice coverage is data-flow-aware and targets the slice.

answer.text: The number of distinct input values explored

feedback.text: That counts inputs, not executed slice statements.

generalfeedback.text: Slice coverage = (executed slice statements) / (total slice statements). The slice is the backward slice of the criterion variable at the output statement.

name.text: What defines the coverage target

questiontext.text: In the app, what defines the coverage target that slice coverage is measured against?

answer.text: The backward slice of the output statement

feedback.text: Correct — the description states the backward slice of the output statement defines the coverage target.

answer.text: The full set of source lines including comments

feedback.text: The target is the backward slice, not every source line.

answer.text: The forward slice of the first input

feedback.text: The app uses the backward slice of the output statement, not a forward slice of an input.

answer.text: The set of all branch outcomes

feedback.text: Slice coverage targets statements in a slice, not branch outcomes.

generalfeedback.text: The backward slice of the output statement defines the coverage target; the learner then toggles traces and watches how much of that slice is exercised.

name.text: Why slice-based adequacy

questiontext.text: Why is slice-based coverage described as a data-flow-aware adequacy criterion?

answer.text: It restricts attention to the statements that actually influence the chosen output

feedback.text: Correct — the backward slice keeps exactly the statements that can affect the output, so coverage focuses on output-relevant code.

answer.text: It counts how many times each loop iterates

feedback.text: Slice coverage is about which slice statements execute, not iteration counts.

answer.text: It ignores data dependences and looks only at control flow

feedback.text: The slice is built from both control and data dependences, so it is data-flow-aware.

answer.text: It measures the size of the input domain

feedback.text: It measures executed slice statements, not the input domain.

generalfeedback.text: A backward slice keeps only statements that can affect the output through control and data dependences, so slice coverage targets output-relevant code — a data-flow-aware adequacy criterion.

name.text: Slice coverage vs statement coverage

questiontext.text: The app shows slice coverage beside plain statement coverage. What is the key difference between the two metrics?

answer.text: Slice coverage is measured only over the slice statements; statement coverage is measured over all statements

feedback.text: Correct — the denominators differ: slice size versus the total number of statements.

answer.text: Slice coverage counts branches while statement coverage counts statements

feedback.text: Both count statements; only the set they are measured over differs.

answer.text: Statement coverage requires a slice; slice coverage does not

feedback.text: The opposite — slice coverage needs the slice; statement coverage uses all statements.

answer.text: They always report the same percentage

feedback.text: They can differ, e.g. in the Classify example a single trace gives different slice and statement percentages.

generalfeedback.text: Slice coverage = executed slice statements / slice size; statement coverage = executed statements / total statements. Same style of count, different reference set.

name.text: What Coverage Gaps lists

questiontext.text: The app's Coverage Gaps panel lists:

answer.text: Slice statements that were not executed by the active traces

feedback.text: Correct — gaps are the uncovered statements of the slice.

answer.text: Statements executed outside the slice

feedback.text: Those are shown separately under "Executed but outside slice", not as gaps.

answer.text: All statements that were executed at least once

feedback.text: Gaps are the uncovered slice statements, not the executed ones.

answer.text: Every branch outcome not taken

feedback.text: The app tracks slice statements, not branch outcomes.

generalfeedback.text: Coverage Gaps are the slice statements that no active trace executed. When none remain, the app reports the output is fully exercised.

name.text: Executed but outside slice

questiontext.text: In the app, the line "Executed but outside slice" lists statements that:

answer.text: Were executed by an active trace but are not part of the slice

feedback.text: Correct — they ran, yet they do not affect the chosen output, so they lie outside the slice.

answer.text: Are in the slice but were never executed

feedback.text: Those are the coverage gaps, not the outside-slice list.

answer.text: Were never executed and are outside the slice

feedback.text: The list requires the statements to have been executed.

answer.text: Are comments and blank lines

feedback.text: Only executable statements are tracked, and these are executed non-slice statements.

generalfeedback.text: Statements executed but outside the slice ran during the traces yet cannot affect the output, so they add to statement coverage without adding to slice coverage.

name.text: The criterion variable

questiontext.text: The app builds the slice as the backward slice of the output statement. Which variable is used as the slicing criterion?

answer.text: The variable used at the output statement (e.g. the returned value)

feedback.text: Correct — the app slices on the variable the output statement reads.

answer.text: Every variable defined anywhere in the program

feedback.text: The criterion is a single variable — the one the output uses.

answer.text: The first input parameter of the function

feedback.text: The criterion is the output's used variable, not an input parameter.

answer.text: A loop counter

feedback.text: The criterion is the variable read at the output statement.

generalfeedback.text: The output statement (kind "output") reads one variable — for example the returned value — and that variable is the slicing criterion for the backward slice.

name.text: Empty slice is vacuously covered

questiontext.text: In the app's metric, a slice that contains no statements is treated as 100% covered.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — an empty slice is vacuously 100% covered, since there is nothing left uncovered.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: With no slice statements to miss, the metric reports 100% by convention.

generalfeedback.text: Slice coverage divides executed slice statements by slice size; when the slice size is zero the app defines the result as 100% (vacuously covered).

name.text: Slice coverage formula

questiontext.text: How does the app compute the slice-coverage percentage?

answer.text: covered slice statements / total slice statements, rounded to a whole percent

feedback.text: Correct — it is the ratio of covered to total slice statements, shown as a rounded percentage with the (covered/total) detail.

answer.text: executed statements / total statements

feedback.text: That is the statement-coverage formula shown on the other row.

answer.text: slice size / total statements

feedback.text: That would measure the slice's relative size, not how much of it is covered.

answer.text: covered slice statements / total statements

feedback.text: The denominator is the slice size, not the total number of statements.

generalfeedback.text: Slice coverage = covered slice statements / slice size, rounded. The app also prints the raw (covered / total) count beside the percentage.

name.text: Read a slice-coverage value (4 of 6)

questiontext.text: The slice-coverage row of the metrics shows the detail (4/6). What percentage does the app display?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 / 6 = 0.667, rounded to 67%.
4 / 6 = 67%, not 46%; do not concatenate the digits.
4 / 6 rounds to 67%, not 60%.
75% would be 3 of 4; here it is 4 of 6 = 67%.

generalfeedback.text: The app rounds covered/total to a whole percent: 4 / 6 = 66.7% -> 67%.

name.text: The two metrics on display

questiontext.text: Which two coverage metrics does the Slice Coverage Explorer display side by side?

answer.text: Slice coverage and statement coverage

feedback.text: Correct — the metrics panel shows a slice-coverage row and a statement-coverage row.

answer.text: Branch coverage and path coverage

feedback.text: The app shows slice and statement coverage, not branch or path.

answer.text: Condition coverage and MC/DC

feedback.text: Those belong to the logic-coverage tools, not this explorer.

answer.text: Mutation score and slice coverage

feedback.text: There is no mutation score here; the second metric is statement coverage.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer contrasts slice coverage with plain statement coverage so you can see how much of what ran is actually output-relevant.

name.text: Read Grade Average with all traces on

questiontext.text: In the Grade Average example every statement lies in the slice, and each trace already reaches all of them. With both traces active, what slice coverage does the app show?

feedback.text: Correct — the whole slice is exercised, so the meter reads 100% (8/8).
All slice statements are covered here, so it is 100%, not 67%.
0% would need no slice statement executed; here every one runs.
The slice is fully covered, giving 100%.

generalfeedback.text: In Grade Average the backward slice of the return value is all 8 statements, and both traces run all of them, so slice coverage is 8/8 = 100%.

name.text: Slice coverage as an adequacy criterion

questiontext.text: Slice coverage is used in the app as a test adequacy criterion. That means it is used to:

answer.text: Judge whether a test suite exercises enough of the output-relevant code

feedback.text: Correct — an adequacy criterion decides when a suite is "good enough" against a target, here the slice.

answer.text: Generate new test inputs automatically

feedback.text: It measures adequacy; it does not generate inputs.

answer.text: Prove the program has no bugs

feedback.text: Coverage shows what ran, not that outputs are correct.

answer.text: Rank inputs by execution time

feedback.text: It is about slice statements exercised, not timing.

generalfeedback.text: An adequacy criterion says when testing is sufficient relative to a goal. Slice coverage judges adequacy against the backward slice of the output.

name.text: Slice can ignore output-irrelevant statements

questiontext.text: A statement that cannot affect the chosen output is excluded from the slice, so leaving it unexecuted does not lower slice coverage.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — only slice statements count toward slice coverage, so output-irrelevant statements do not affect it.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Statements outside the slice do not affect the output and are not counted in slice coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Slice coverage is measured only over the backward slice. Statements that cannot reach the output are outside the slice, so their execution status does not change slice coverage (though it can still change statement coverage).

name.text: Effect of toggling a trace off

questiontext.text: In the app, toggling one trace chip off:

answer.text: Removes that trace's executed statements from the union, possibly lowering both metrics

feedback.text: Correct — the executed set is the union over active traces, so dropping one can uncover slice statements.

answer.text: Deletes those statements from the program

feedback.text: The program is unchanged; only the set of active traces changes.

answer.text: Recomputes the slice from scratch

feedback.text: The slice depends on the output criterion, not on which traces are active.

answer.text: Always raises slice coverage

feedback.text: Removing a trace can only keep or lower the covered set, never raise it.

generalfeedback.text: The executed set is the union of steps across all active traces. Turning a trace off shrinks that union, so covered slice statements can only stay the same or decrease.

name.text: Classify: size of the output slice

questiontext.text:
Consider the Classify example:

function classify(n) {
  let label = "zero";     // s2
  let sign  = 0;          // s3
  if (n > 0) {           // s4
    label = "positive";   // s5
    sign  = 1;            // s6
  } else if (n < 0) {    // s7
    label = "negative";   // s8
    sign  = -1;           // s9
  }
  return label;           // s11
}

There are 9 executable statements. How many statements are in the backward slice of the returned label?

feedback.text: Correct — the slice is {s2, s4, s5, s7, s8, s11}; the three sign assignments are excluded.
The three sign statements (s3, s6, s9) do not affect label, so the slice is 6, not all 9.
3 is the number of statements excluded (the sign assignments); the slice keeps the other 6.
The slice is {s2, s4, s5, s7, s8, s11} = 6 statements.

generalfeedback.text: label is defined at s2/s5/s8, guarded by the decisions s4/s7, and returned at s11: slice = {s2, s4, s5, s7, s8, s11} = 6 of 9.

name.text: Classify: statements outside the slice

questiontext.text: In the Classify example, which statements are not in the backward slice of label?

answer.text: s3, s6, s9 — the three sign assignments

feedback.text: Correct — sign never flows into label, so those three statements are outside the slice.

answer.text: s4, s7 — the two decisions

feedback.text: The decisions control which label assignment runs, so they are in the slice.

answer.text: s2, s11 — the initialisation and the return

feedback.text: Both write or read label, so they are in the slice.

answer.text: s5, s8 — the branch labels

feedback.text: These assign label, so they are in the slice.

generalfeedback.text: The slice of label excludes s3, s6, s9 because sign has no data or control path to the returned label.

name.text: Classify: slice coverage of the positive trace

questiontext.text: In Classify, activate only the n=5 ("positive") trace. It executes s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s11. The slice is {s2, s4, s5, s7, s8, s11}. What slice coverage does the app show?

feedback.text: Correct — it covers s2, s4, s5, s11 of the slice (4 of 6) = 67%.
The positive trace misses s7 and s8, so only 4 of 6 slice statements are covered.
s7 and s8 (the negative branch) are never executed, so it cannot be 100%.
67% is right but the count is over the slice (4/6), not all statements (6/9 is statement coverage).

generalfeedback.text: The positive trace covers slice statements s2, s4, s5, s11 but misses s7 and s8, so slice coverage = 4/6 = 67%.

name.text: Classify: slice coverage of the negative trace

questiontext.text: In Classify, activate only the n=-3 ("negative") trace. It executes s2, s3, s4, s7, s8, s9, s11. The slice is {s2, s4, s5, s7, s8, s11}. What slice coverage is shown?

feedback.text: Correct — it covers s2, s4, s7, s8, s11 (5 of 6); only s5 is missed.
The negative trace reaches s7 and s8, so 5 of 6 slice statements are covered.
s5 (the positive-branch label) is never executed, so it is 5/6, not 6/6.
78% is this trace's statement coverage; slice coverage is 5/6 = 83%.

generalfeedback.text: The negative trace covers s2, s4, s7, s8, s11 and misses only s5, so slice coverage = 5/6 = 83%.

name.text: Classify: slice coverage of the zero trace

questiontext.text: In Classify, activate only the n=0 ("zero") trace. It executes s2, s3, s4, s7, s11. The slice is {s2, s4, s5, s7, s8, s11}. What slice coverage is shown?

feedback.text: Correct — it covers s2, s4, s7, s11 (4 of 6); s5 and s8 are missed.
56% is this trace's statement coverage; slice coverage is measured over the 6 slice statements = 4/6 = 67%.
Both s5 and s8 are missed, so only 4 of 6 slice statements are covered.
Four slice statements run (s2, s4, s7, s11), giving 4/6 = 67%.

generalfeedback.text: The zero trace never enters either label-changing branch, so it covers s2, s4, s7, s11 and misses s5 and s8: slice coverage = 4/6 = 67%.

name.text: Classify: statement coverage of the positive trace

questiontext.text: In Classify (9 executable statements), activate only the n=5 trace, which executes s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s11 (6 statements). What statement coverage does the app show?

feedback.text: Correct — 6 of the 9 statements execute, so 6/9 = 67%.
4/6 is the slice coverage; statement coverage is over all 9 statements = 6/9.
The negative branch (s7, s8, s9) never runs, so it is 6/9, not 9/9.
The positive trace runs 6 statements, not 7, so 6/9 = 67%.

generalfeedback.text: Statement coverage = executed / total = 6/9 = 67%. Note the slice coverage happens to also be 67% here, but it is measured over a different set (4/6).

name.text: Classify: statement coverage of the negative trace

questiontext.text: In Classify (9 statements), activate only the n=-3 trace, which executes s2, s3, s4, s7, s8, s9, s11 (7 statements). What statement coverage is shown?

feedback.text: Correct — 7 of 9 statements execute, so 7/9 = 78%.
83% is this trace's slice coverage; statement coverage is 7/9 = 78%.
The negative trace executes 7 statements, not 6, so 7/9 = 78%.
The positive branch (s5, s6) never runs, so it is 7/9, not 9/9.

generalfeedback.text: Statement coverage = 7/9 = 78%. The slice coverage for the same trace is 5/6 = 83%, higher because the missed non-slice statement s6 does not count against the slice.

name.text: Classify: gaps under the positive trace

questiontext.text: In Classify, with only the n=5 ("positive") trace active, which slice statements appear in the Coverage Gaps panel?

answer.text: s7 and s8 — the negative-branch decision and label

answer.text: None — the slice is fully covered

feedback.text: s7 and s8 are never reached, so two gaps remain.

name.text: Classify: why sign=1 is outside the slice

feedback.text: s6 does execute in the positive trace; it is excluded because it cannot affect label, not because it never runs.

answer.text: Because it assigns a constant

name.text: Classify: executed but outside slice under positive

questiontext.text: In Classify, with only the n=5 trace active, which statements does the app list under "Executed but outside slice"?

answer.text: s3 and s6

answer.text: s7 and s8

name.text: Match term to role

questiontext.text: In the Slice Coverage Explorer, which term-to-role pairing is correct?

answer.text: Backward slice = the coverage target; a gap = an uncovered slice statement

feedback.text: Correct — the slice is what must be covered, and a gap is a slice statement no active trace reached.

answer.text: Executed set = the coverage target; a gap = a non-slice statement

feedback.text: The target is the slice, not the executed set, and a gap is an uncovered slice statement.

answer.text: Slice = the executed union; outside-slice = an uncovered slice statement

feedback.text: The slice is the target, not the executed union, and outside-slice statements were executed, not uncovered.

answer.text: Statement coverage = slice size; gap = a taken branch

feedback.text: Statement coverage is executed/total, and a gap is an uncovered slice statement, not a branch.

generalfeedback.text: Slice = coverage target; executed set = union of active traces' steps; gap = uncovered slice statement; outside-slice = executed statement not in the slice.

name.text: Classify: fewest traces for full slice coverage

questiontext.text: In Classify, which set of traces is the smallest that reaches 100% slice coverage?

name.text: Classify: statement coverage of the zero trace

questiontext.text: In Classify (9 statements), activate only the n=0 trace, which executes s2, s3, s4, s7, s11 (5 statements). What statement coverage is shown?

4/6 is the slice coverage; statement coverage is 5/9 = 56%.

name.text: Classify: why the negative trace's slice % exceeds its statement %

answer.text: The slice is larger than the set of all statements

feedback.text: The slice (6) is smaller than all statements (9); the difference is which misses count.

answer.text: Slice coverage rounds up while statement coverage rounds down

answer.text: The trace executes more slice statements than total statements

name.text: Classify: what the zero trace's two gaps reveal

questiontext.text: In Classify, the n=0 trace gives slice coverage 67% (4/6) with gaps s5 and s8. What do these two gaps reveal about the suite?

answer.text: Neither the positive-label case nor the negative-label case is exercised, so both label-changing paths are untested

answer.text: The return statement was never reached

questiontext.text: In Classify, if you may activate only one trace, which gives the highest slice coverage?

answer.text: The negative trace (n=-3), at 83%

name.text: Subset implication between the metrics

questiontext.text: Because the backward slice is a subset of all statements, which implication always holds?

answer.text: 100% statement coverage guarantees 100% slice coverage, but not the reverse

feedback.text: Correct — if every statement ran, every slice statement ran; but full slice coverage can leave non-slice statements unexecuted.

answer.text: 100% slice coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage

feedback.text: Reversed — covering the slice says nothing about statements outside it.

answer.text: The two percentages are always equal

feedback.text: They differ whenever the slice is a proper subset, as in Classify.

answer.text: Neither can ever reach 100% unless the other does

feedback.text: Slice coverage can be 100% while statement coverage is below 100%.

generalfeedback.text: Slice statements are a subset of all statements. Executing all statements executes all slice statements (statement 100% => slice 100%); the converse fails because non-slice statements may stay unexecuted.

name.text: Classify: positive + zero result and remaining gap

Neither trace enters the negative branch, so s8 stays uncovered.

answer.text: 67% (4/6), with s7 and s8 uncovered

feedback.text: The zero trace covers s7, so only s8 remains — 5/6 = 83%.

answer.text: 83% (5/6), with s5 still uncovered

feedback.text: s5 is covered by the positive trace; the remaining gap is s8.

generalfeedback.text: positive covers s5; zero covers s7. Their union covers s2, s4, s5, s7, s11 = 5 of 6. Only s8 (negative label) is missed, so 83% with gap s8.

name.text: Grade Average: why the metrics coincide

answer.text: They are always equal, because the slice equals the full statement set

feedback.text: Correct — with slice = all statements, both metrics have the same numerator and denominator for every suite.

answer.text: Slice coverage is always higher

feedback.text: They coincide exactly, because the reference sets are identical here.

answer.text: Statement coverage is always higher

feedback.text: Neither is higher; the two figures are equal when the slice is the whole program.

answer.text: They are unrelated

feedback.text: They are identical here because the slice contains every statement.

generalfeedback.text: When the slice equals the full statement set, executed-slice/slice-size = executed/total for every suite, so the two metrics report the same percentage.

name.text: What a slice gap reveals over a green bar

questiontext.text: What diagnostic value does a slice-coverage gap add beyond a high statement-coverage bar?

answer.text: It pinpoints an unexecuted statement that actually affects the output, focusing attention on output-relevant untested code

feedback.text: Correct — a gap is an uncovered statement inside the slice, so it is known to influence the output.

answer.text: It proves the executed statements produce correct outputs

feedback.text: Coverage never proves correctness, only what ran.

answer.text: It counts how many inputs were tried

feedback.text: A gap is a slice statement, not an input count.

answer.text: It measures execution time of the slice

feedback.text: Gaps are about coverage of slice statements, not timing.

generalfeedback.text: Statement coverage can look high while missing output-relevant code hidden among many irrelevant statements. A slice gap flags exactly an output-affecting statement still untested.

name.text: Slice coverage vs branch coverage

questiontext.text: How does slice coverage differ in intent from branch (decision) coverage?

answer.text: Slice coverage targets the statements that affect a chosen output; branch coverage targets each decision's true/false outcomes regardless of the output

feedback.text: Correct — slice coverage is output-directed and data-flow-aware, while branch coverage is about decision outcomes.

answer.text: They measure the same thing under different names

feedback.text: They differ: one is a data-flow slice target, the other counts branch outcomes.

answer.text: Slice coverage counts branch outcomes; branch coverage counts statements

feedback.text: Reversed — slice coverage counts slice statements, not branch outcomes.

answer.text: Branch coverage requires a slice; slice coverage does not

feedback.text: Branch coverage needs no slice; slice coverage is the one built on the backward slice.

generalfeedback.text: Branch coverage asks whether each decision took both outcomes. Slice coverage asks whether the statements that can affect a chosen output were exercised — a data-flow-aware, output-directed goal.

name.text: Classify: what the negative-trace gap implies

questiontext.text: In Classify, the n=-3 trace leaves exactly one gap, s5 (label = "positive"). What does this gap imply for fault detection?

answer.text: A fault in how the positive label is assigned could go undetected, since no active test exercises s5

feedback.text: Correct — an uncovered slice statement means a defect there would not be exercised by the suite.

answer.text: The negative label is untested

feedback.text: The negative label s8 is covered by this trace; the gap is the positive label s5.

answer.text: The return value is never produced

feedback.text: s11 runs; the gap is s5, the positive-branch assignment.

answer.text: Nothing — a single gap does not matter

feedback.text: An uncovered slice statement is exactly where a fault could hide from the suite.

generalfeedback.text: s5 assigns the positive label. With only the negative trace active, s5 never runs, so a bug in the positive-label case would not be caught until a positive input is added.

name.text: Classify: can one trace reach full slice coverage?

questiontext.text: In Classify, can any single trace reach 100% slice coverage?

answer.text: No — s5 and s8 are on mutually exclusive branches, so at least two traces are needed

feedback.text: Correct — a single input takes one branch, so it can reach s5 or s8 but not both; the best single trace is 83%.

answer.text: Yes — the negative trace alone reaches 100%

feedback.text: The negative trace misses s5, giving 83%, not 100%.

answer.text: Yes — the zero trace alone reaches 100%

feedback.text: The zero trace misses both s5 and s8, giving only 67%.

answer.text: No — because the slice is empty

feedback.text: The slice has 6 statements; the reason is that s5 and s8 lie on exclusive branches.

generalfeedback.text: s5 (positive) and s8 (negative) are on exclusive branches, so no single input covers both. Two traces (positive + negative) are required for 100%.

name.text: Classify: value of covering the sign statements

questiontext.text: In Classify, with all traces active both metrics read 100%. For the slice (label) criterion, what does exercising the sign statements (s3, s6, s9) add?

answer.text: Nothing — they are outside the slice, so they do not contribute to slice adequacy for label

feedback.text: Correct — sign cannot affect label, so covering those statements does not improve slice coverage of the label criterion.

answer.text: They are required to reach 100% slice coverage

feedback.text: They are outside the slice, so they are irrelevant to slice coverage of label.

answer.text: They raise the slice size to 9

feedback.text: The slice stays at 6; non-slice statements are never added to it.

answer.text: They flip the slice coverage from 100% to 67%

feedback.text: Non-slice statements never change slice coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Slice coverage of label is measured only over the 6 slice statements. Exercising s3, s6, s9 raises statement coverage but adds nothing to slice adequacy for the label criterion.

name.text: Grade Average: redundancy for the slice criterion

questiontext.text: In Grade Average, each trace on its own already yields 100% slice coverage. For the slice (return-value) criterion, what does that say about the second trace?

answer.text: It is redundant for slice coverage — one trace already fully exercises the slice

feedback.text: Correct — if one trace covers the whole slice, adding another adds no slice coverage.

answer.text: It is required to reach 100% slice coverage

feedback.text: A single trace already reaches 100%, so the second is not required for slice coverage.

answer.text: It lowers slice coverage

feedback.text: Adding a trace can only keep or raise the covered set, never lower it.

answer.text: It changes the slice

feedback.text: The slice depends on the output criterion, not on active traces.

generalfeedback.text: Both Grade Average traces reach all 8 slice statements, so for the slice criterion the second trace is redundant — though it may still add value for other goals (e.g. different data values).

name.text: Classify: combining two 67% traces

questiontext.text: In Classify, the positive and zero traces each give 67% slice coverage, but with different gaps (positive misses s7, s8; zero misses s5, s8). Activating both together gives what, and why not 100%?

answer.text: 83% — together they cover s5 and s7, but s8 is missed by both

feedback.text: Correct — s8 (the negative label) is in neither trace, so one gap remains: 5/6 = 83%.

answer.text: 100% — their gaps are complementary

feedback.text: Both miss s8, so the union is not complete; it is 83%.

answer.text: 67% — combining traces cannot raise coverage

feedback.text: Combining traces unions their covered sets, so it can raise coverage; here to 83%.

answer.text: 134% — the percentages add

feedback.text: Coverage is a fraction of one slice, capped at 100%; you union the covered sets, not add percentages.

generalfeedback.text: positive covers s5; zero covers s7; both miss s8. Their union covers 5 of 6 slice statements = 83%, so equal single-trace percentages can still leave a shared gap.

name.text: Why "data-flow-aware" adequacy

questiontext.text: Slice coverage is called a data-flow-aware adequacy criterion because the target set is built by:

answer.text: Following control and data dependences backward from the output to keep exactly the statements that can affect it

feedback.text: Correct — the backward slice traces dependences to the output, so the criterion is defined by data (and control) flow.

answer.text: Listing every source line in file order

feedback.text: The slice follows dependences, not textual order.

answer.text: Enumerating all branch outcomes

feedback.text: That describes branch coverage, which is not built from a data-flow slice.

answer.text: Sampling random inputs and recording crashes

feedback.text: That is fuzzing; slice coverage is defined by the dependence structure.

generalfeedback.text: The backward slice is computed by walking control- and data-dependence edges from the output statement. Because that walk is driven by data flow, slice coverage is a data-flow-aware criterion.

name.text: Classify: equal percentages, different meaning

questiontext.text: In Classify, the positive trace shows slice coverage 67% (4/6) and statement coverage 67% (6/9) — the same percentage. What is the correct reading?

answer.text: The equal percentages are a coincidence of the ratios; the two metrics count different sets (4 of 6 slice statements vs 6 of 9 total)

feedback.text: Correct — 4/6 and 6/9 both round to 67%, yet they measure coverage over different reference sets.

answer.text: The slice and the statement set must be identical here

feedback.text: They are not — the slice is 6 statements, the full set is 9.

answer.text: Equal percentages mean the same statements were covered

feedback.text: Not necessarily; the counts are over different sets, so equal percentages do not imply the same statements.

answer.text: One of the figures must be a display error

feedback.text: Both are correct; 4/6 = 6/9 = 66.7% -> 67%.

generalfeedback.text: 4/6 and 6/9 both equal 0.667, so both show 67%. The equality is arithmetic coincidence; slice coverage is over the 6 slice statements while statement coverage is over all 9.
